title: Write the boilerplate a record saves you

blocks.text: The one line `record Person(String name, int age) {}` gives you a constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. A traditional class has to write them by hand, and every hand-written one is a chance for a mistake.
`PersonBean` is the traditional-class version of that record: its fields, constructor and accessors are written. Write the other three so that a `PersonBean` behaves exactly like the record would:

items: `equals(Object)`: `true` for another `PersonBean` with an equal `name` (which may be `null`) and the same `age`; `false` for `null` and for any other type;
`hashCode()`: equal beans have equal hash codes (`Objects.hash` helps);

blocks.text:
new PersonBean("Alice", 30).equals(new PersonBean("Alice", 30))   -> true
new PersonBean("Alice", 30).equals(new PersonBean("Alice", 31))   -> false
new PersonBean(null, 5).equals(new PersonBean(null, 5))           -> true
new PersonBean("Alice", 30).equals("Alice")                       -> false
new PersonBean("Alice", 30).toString()                            -> "PersonBean[name=Alice, age=30]"

cases.says: Equal components make equal beans, and toString reads PersonBean[name=Alice, age=30].
Beans with a null name compare and hash without a NullPointerException.
Equal beans have equal hash codes, so a HashSet holds one of them.
A bean is not equal to null or to an object of another type, and saying so throws nothing.

concepts: A record generates the equals, hashCode and toString a traditional class must write by hand, and hand-written ones are where errors creep in.
